articles.body:
An explosive first inning propelled the Chicago White Sox to a Game 1 victory over the Houston Astros in their American League Wild Card matchup Tuesday, as Chicago secured a 6-3 win on the road behind a standout performance from Munetaka Murakami.

The Astros entered Tuesday's matchup as 1.5-point favorites, according to FanDuel Sportsbook , but were unable to capitalize on their home-field advantage.

Houston starter AJ Blubaugh struggled from the outset, allowing three walks and an RBI on 27 pitches before being pulled with the first inning still in progress.

MLB.com has released the complete playoff schedule, including dates and information on where to watch each game.

A rocky first inning from the Astros' pitching staff helped the White Sox jump out to an early 1-0 lead, with Murakami delivering a sacrifice fly to bring home Sam Antonacci for the game's first run.

Chicago continued to build on its momentum on the road, adding four more runs while keeping Houston off the scoreboard through the fifth inning.

Antonacci added two RBIs in the second inning, while Chase Meidroth drove in another run in the fifth. Colson Montgomery also got in on the action, launching a solo home run to center field in the fourth to extend the White Sox's lead.

Nelson Velazquez provided a much-needed spark for Houston in Game 1, launching a two-run homer in the fifth inning to finally put the Astros on the scoreboard and cut the White Sox's lead to 5-2.

Houston's pitching struggles continued to hurt the Astros, as a wild pitch in the seventh inning allowed Chicago's Murakami to score from third. The run extended the White Sox's advantage to 6-2.

José Altuve came through for Houston with two outs, racing through first base on an infield single that brought home a run and trimmed the deficit to 6-3 heading into the final inning.

The Astros and closer Josh Hader kept the White Sox off the scoreboard in the top of the ninth, giving Houston a final opportunity to erase the deficit and either tie the game or take the lead.

Christian Walker drew a walk and advanced to second, but Houston could not produce a late-game rally. Velazquez was unable to replicate his earlier heroics, grounding out to record the final out and seal a 6-3 Game 1 victory for the White Sox.

With a chance to sweep the Astros and advance 2-0 in the AL Wild Card Series, the White Sox will remain the road team in Houston on Wednesday for Game 2. First pitch is scheduled for 5:00 p.m. ET, with the game available to stream on Peacock and watch on NBCSN.

articles.title: White Sox take down Astros as Grant Taylor delivers, Houston bullpen implodes in wild-card Game 1
articles.summary: Taylor's 7-out save sealed the victory for Chicago and put Houston on the brink of elimination.
articles.body:
Two bullpen games entered. One disintegrated almost immediately.

Game 1 of the American League wild-card series between the Chicago White Sox and Houston Astros did not feature the caliber of pitching typically associated with a postseason series opener. Not only were these the two weakest teams to qualify for the postseason , but also both clubs exhausted their top arms this past weekend as they continued to chase division titles. Astros ace Hunter Brown and White Sox innings leader Sean Burke both pitched Friday, making a Tuesday turnaround too tight.

As such, it was a pair of rookies in Houston right-hander AJ Blubaugh and Chicago lefty Hagen Smith who squared off as the de facto starting pitchers in Game 1. They served as the opening acts for a parade of relievers to follow, as the two undermanned clubs sought the 27 outs required to begin their postseason run on the right foot. The White Sox emerged victorious, taking Game 1 by a score of 6-3 .

Unfortunately for Houston, the bullpen door had to open even earlier than planned. Blubaugh lost the strike zone in the top of the first inning, sending the Astros' mound strategy spiraling from the get-go. Blubaugh — who led major-league relievers in innings pitched in the regular season, with a whopping 96 frames across 64 appearances, but was making his first start of the year — walked three of the five batters he faced and recorded only two outs before he was replaced by left-hander Bryan King . Prior to that, a throwing error from first baseman Christian Walker allowed leadoff man Sam Antonacci (who walked) to reach third base and eventually score on a sacrifice fly from Munetaka Murakami that gave Chicago a 1-0 lead.

It was a sloppy start all around for the 81-win Astros, the worst division winner in modern baseball history .

King escaped the top of the first with the Astros down only 1-0, but he struggled upon returning to the mound. Five straight Chicago hitters reached to open the second inning, a stretch that included a two-RBI single from Antonacci. Once again, Astros manager Joe Espada needed to make a pitching change before he would've liked, calling on another rookie in right-hander Miguel Ullola to clean up the mess. Ullola succeeded in keeping the score 3-0, but the damage was already done, and the Astros' bats were making minimal progress rallying back.

Chicago's bullpen adventure got off to a much smoother start thanks to Smith, who emerged down the stretch as a valuable multi-inning weapon. The fifth overall pick in 2024 — those White Sox were 27-71 on the day he was drafted — Smith was selected with the idea that he could one day start a postseason game, once the Sox launched themselves out of their deep rebuild. These likely weren't quite the circumstances the organization envisioned; Smith still has a lot to prove to become a reliable major-league starting pitcher. But the 23-year-old was up to the task Tuesday, providing three scoreless innings, including coaxing a pair of harmless groundouts from AL MVP favorite Yordan Alvarez .

Shortly after Smith strolled off the mound the third time, the White Sox got their biggest swing of the game courtesy of Colson Montgomery . The 24-year-old shortstop was batting ninth for Chicago, dropped to the bottom of the batting order after finishing the regular season on a miserable 4-for-62 skid that saw him break the MLB record for strikeouts in a season, with 227 .

But Montgomery has titanic, left-handed power. It was lying dormant during his brutal slump, but it produced 31 home runs before that, making him a uniquely dangerous threat at the bottom of Chicago's lineup. And leading off the fourth, Montgomery reminded everyone of his prodigious pop, crushing an 0-2 fastball up and away from Ullola to straightaway center field for a 432-foot solo homer that made it 4-0 White Sox.

From there, Chicago's ride to the finish was a little bumpy, giving the ultra-young roster its first taste of the nerve-wracking nature of postseason baseball. Nelson Velazquez got the Astros on the board in the fifth with a pinch-hit, two-run homer off Sean Newcomb that made it 5-2, but Chicago responded with an insurance run a couple of innings later, when left-hander Bennett Sousa — Houston's sixth pitcher — uncorked a wild pitch that enabled Murakami to scamper home from third.

The Astros produced some more pressure in the eighth inning — a two-out Jose Altuve RBI infield single made it 6-3 — but White Sox right-hander Grant Taylor navigated the jam with a nasty strikeout of Yainer Diaz to strand two runners.

Taylor returned for the ninth and worked around a leadoff walk to wrap up an impressive seven-out save, finishing with 54 pitches — the highest pitch count of his major-league career and the most he has thrown since he tossed 59 in Double-A on April 16, 2025. It was quite the effort from Chicago's best bullpen arm and a worthy one to nail down a Game 1 victory, though it likely renders him unavailable for Game 2 on Wednesday.

The White Sox won't be alone in possibly dealing with a limited bullpen. Although the Astros' eighth-inning rally was cut short, it was enough to motivate Espada to bring in closer Josh Hader for the top of the ninth despite trailing three runs. Hader threw only 11 pitches in a scoreless frame, but if the Astros are counting on him to close out the next two games, should Houston rally back, that would mean asking Hader to do something he hasn't done since September 2023: pitch three days in a row.

But those are problems for tomorrow and Thursday. For now, all Houston can do is reset and hope Brown can deliver an ace-like effort in Game 2 and limit the beleaguered bullpen's exposure, whether or not that includes Hader. The White Sox will give the ball to Burke, who doesn't wield the high-powered arsenal of Brown but has been a steady presence atop Chicago's rotation all season.

It took until Game 162 for the Astros to know for sure they'd be playing in the postseason. Now they're facing elimination before the calendar even flips to October.

articles.title: Giancarlo Stanton Gives Injury Update After Being Named to Yankees' MLB Wild Card Roster vs. Red Sox
articles.summary: New York Yankees slugger Giancarlo Stanton confirmed that he'll be available as a pinch hitter during the team's American League Wild Card Series clash with the Boston Red Sox.
articles.body:
New York Yankees slugger Giancarlo Stanton confirmed that he'll be available as a pinch hitter during the team's American League Wild Card Series clash with the Boston Red Sox.

"Ready to go," Stanton told Jon Heyman of the New York Post . "I'll help the team any way I can. It's the most exciting time of the year."

While Stanton hasn't appeared in a game since April 24 due to calf issues, he was included as part of the Yankees' 26-man roster for the Wild Card round.

The five-time All-Star initially suffered a right calf strain before experiencing multiple setbacks throughout his rehab, which included a strain of his left calf.

Stanton has continued to deal with injuries in recent years, appearing in just 101 of a possible 324 regular-season contests since the start of his 2025 campaign.

Yankees manager Aaron Boone was impressed with the 36-year-old's recovery from his latest health woes, though.

"This has obviously been a trying year for him on the injury front, having a couple of setbacks along the way," Boone said, per MLB.com's Bryan Hoch . "He's never stopped going and stopped grinding, even through some tough moments.

"This is a unique series in that we feel like we're able to go heavy on the position player front. There's an avenue for him for an at-bat, some interchangeable parts there. So credit to him for putting himself in position to be an option."

Despite Stanton's availability concerns, he's consistently stepped up for the Yankees during the playoffs.

In 48 career postseason games, he owns a .254/.322/.605 slash line with eight doubles and 18 home runs. He also earned ALCS MVP honors for New York in 2024.

While Yankees star Aaron Judge wasn't included on their Wild Card roster as he continues to work his way back from his own calf issue , Stanton is available for the Bronx Bombers.

articles.title: White Sox's Sean Burke Drops Legendary Quote Ahead of MLB Wild Card Game 2 Start vs. Astros
articles.summary: Sean Burke led the Chicago White Sox in innings pitched this season and will take the ball Wednesday with a chance to close out the Houston Astros in Game 2 of their Wild Card Series.
articles.body:
Sean Burke led the Chicago White Sox in innings pitched this season and will take the ball Wednesday with a chance to close out the Houston Astros in Game 2 of their Wild Card Series.

"This is my life," he told James Fegan of the Chicago Sun-Times . "I don't have family, no girl, no kids. This is all I do."

He did it well this season, posting a 3.34 ERA, 1.20 WHIP and 185 strikeouts in 172.1 innings. It was quite an improvement from the 2025 campaign when he finished with a 4.22 ERA and 1.44 WHIP for a White Sox club that finished in last place in the American League Central.

Chicago went from three straight seasons with more than 100 losses to the playoffs in 2026 in no small part because of Burke's reliability. Now he will be tasked with starting his first postseason game and has a golden opportunity to help his team advance to the Division Series.

After all, the momentum is on the White Sox's side after Tuesday's 6-3 victory.

They threw five different pitchers with Hagen Smith serving as the opener and going three innings. From there, Jordan Hicks, Sean Newcomb, David Sandlin and Grant Taylor went the rest of the way.

Houston took a similar strategy and ended up pitching eight different arms with nobody going longer than three innings.

If Burke pitches as the White Sox hope in Game 2, it will have a much more traditional feel with fewer bullpen arms taking the mound and a starter going deep into the game.

It would likely also mean the end of the series after just two contests.

articles.title: Yankees' Cam Schlittler Has Become the Red Sox Worst Nightmare
articles.summary: The most lopsided "rivalry" in sports history is the Harlem Globetrotters against the Washington Generals, the former defeating the latter in more than 99.9 percent of their more than 16,000 exhibitions.
articles.body:
The most lopsided "rivalry" in sports history is the Harlem Globetrotters against the Washington Generals, the former defeating the latter in more than 99.9 percent of their more than 16,000 exhibitions.

But the second-most lopsided rivalry has quickly become Cam Schlittler's dominance of the Boston Red Sox.

Even before Schlittler's first career appearance against the Red Sox in last year's wild card round, it was a full-blown narrative that the Yankees had found a budding star who was born and raised in East Walpole, Massachusetts, before playing college ball at Boston's Northeastern University—where the Red Sox never bothered to scout him much.

After some Red Sox fans harassed Schlittler and his family on social media in advance of that game, it became personal.

He eviscerated Boston a year ago in eight shutout innings with 12 strikeouts in a winner-take-all affair. It was one of the most dominant postseason performances in pitching history.

He faced Boston four times in the 2026 regular season, allowing just two earned runs in 24.1 innings. That's a 0.74 ERA, along with a 0.99 WHIP and 10.0 K/9.

But it appears he really loves facing Boston in the postseason, delivering another 6.1 scoreless innings with 10 strikeouts and just two hits allowed in Tuesday night's 9-0 Game 1 victory.

Schlittler set the tone early, striking out the side in the first inning.

It did take him 22 pitches to get out of the first, thanks to a 10-pitch AB by Adley Rutschman that ended with an opposite-field single. But perhaps more than the strikeouts, that battle showed how hard it would be to muster anything at all against the man who will be named the AL Cy Young winner in about six weeks.

After Rutschman's single, Schlittler retired 18 of the next 19 batters, with a Jarren Duran walk the only reason he had to pitch out of the stretch.

Schlittler set a career high with 24 swings and misses, 14 of which came against his four-seamer.

The real story, though, was the curveball that he threw a staggering 32 times. His previous high was 20, usually the fourth-most utilized pitch in his arsenal. But that Uncle Charlie was so lethal on the first two strikeouts to Roman Anthony and Willson Contreras that he couldn't help but keep going back to it.

At that point, the scouting notebook was worthless to the Red Sox.

Although given the history of Schlittler vs. Boston, perhaps it already was.

Factoring in the two postseason starts, Schlittler's career line against the Red Sox now stands at: 38.2 IP, 22 H, 2 ER, 10 BB, 49 K; 0.47 ERA, 0.83 WHIP, 11.4 K/9

That's an "Are we sure that kid is only 12?" Little League World Series-type of pitching line.

Pretty sure that guy who went viral two months ago for trying to throw a perfect game with Roy Oswalt in MVP Baseball 2005 wasn't even that unhittable.

But it has already become business as usual in just his second season in the bigs.

Schlittler couldn't beat the Red Sox by himself, though. Only Shohei Ohtani could pull off something like that.

He needed some run support to get the win, and adding to Boston's "How did we miss on that guy?" misery, Ben Rice (from Cohasset, Massachusetts) delivered some postseason history of his own with four hits, two home runs and six RBI.

During the regular season, Rice had a .473 OPS against the Red Sox, striking out in 16 of his 46 plate appearances. But like Schlittler, he grew up as a Yankees fan behind enemy lines, and he sure did bring the goods when it mattered most.

After nearly two months of preparing ourselves for this inevitable clash of the Northeast titans?

If you watched any of the games on Tuesday, you might have heard a dozen or so times that, in the first four years of this 12-team postseason format, the team that won Game 1 of the wild card round won the series 15 of 16 times, most of them in sweeps.

The lone exception to that rule, though?

Last year's Yankees-Red Sox battle, in which the Yankees lost the opener to Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet before coming back to win Games 2 and 3.

Unfortunately for Boston, there shall be no rest for the wicked.

The 2025 Yankees came back by putting a hurtin' on Brayan Bello and Connelly Early—two zero-time All-Stars who otherwise have never pitched in the postseason.

The Red Sox, meanwhile, will need to rally against Max Fried and Gerrit Cole.

And, well, Fried has owned Boston almost as completely as Schlittler has, with a 1.24 ERA in seven starts over the past two years.

articles.title: Cam Schlittler Reacts to MVP Chants After Historic Start for Yankees in Wild Card Win vs. Red Sox
articles.summary: Cam Schlittler appreciates the New York Yankees fans, but he doesn't think he is an MVP just because they were chanting as much during Tuesday's 9-0 victory over the Boston Red Sox in Game 1 of their Wild Card Series.
articles.body:
Cam Schlittler appreciates the New York Yankees fans, but he doesn't think he is an MVP just because they were chanting as much during Tuesday's 9-0 victory over the Boston Red Sox in Game 1 of their Wild Card Series.

"We've already got an MVP in this locker room, he's won three of them," he told reporters while referencing Aaron Judge. "… It's a good feeling. I wouldn't say I am an MVP, but it's good to embrace that from the fans."

Schlittler may not think he's an MVP, but he looked like one Monday.

He allowed just two hits and one walk while striking out 10 in 6.1 innings of work. It was a brilliant individual performance and set the tone against the Yankees' archrivals right out of the gates in their short series.

It was also more of the same after he finished the regular season with a 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP and 239 strikeouts in 193.2 innings. He will surely take home the American League Cy Young award for his efforts, but his ultimate legacy may come down to what he does in the playoffs.

And he couldn't have scripted a much better start.

New York didn't need much offense behind Schlittler but it got plenty anyway with Ben Rice going 4-for-5 with two home runs and six RBI. Throw in two RBI from Austin Wells, and the Yankees gave their dominant right-hander more than enough run support.

With Judge sidelined by injury, New York needed others to play like MVPs to take an early series lead.

Schlittler and Rice did just that, and now the team is one win away from advancing to the Division Series.

articles.title: Michael King flirts with no-hitter as Padres dominate Cubs in wild-card Game 1
articles.summary: The Padres' starter didn't allow a hit until the seventh inning. The game was a rout by then.
articles.body: The San Diego Padres ended the regular season as the hottest team in baseball. It's how they started the postseason, too.Michael King flirted with a no-hitter, Fernando Tatis Jr. had a vintage performance, and plenty of other players contributed to an 8-0 Padres win over the Chicago Cubs to open their wild-card series. Game 2 is scheduled for Wednesday at 7 p.m. PT.The game Tuesday was the largest shutout win in Padres postseason history.The tone was set as early as the first inning, when King struck out Cubs stars Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman, then Tatis and Manny Machado clubbed home runs off Cubs starter Matthew Boyd. Petco Park grew more euphoric with every beat, and the home fans didn't have much reason to lose that high over the next eight innings.Fernando Tatis Jr. and the Padres crowd knew on contact 🔥 pic.twitter.com/mtZMh4BTst— MLB (@MLB) September 30, 2026 Even with the lopsided score, King's performance meant the game was worth watching into the seventh inning. The right-hander, who rejoined the Padres last winter on a deal clearly designed to let him establish his value for another go at free agency this coming offseason, took a no-hitter into the seventh inning.He did so despite facing a Cubs team that led MLB in runs scored in the regular season and went 5-1 against the Padres with 9.2 runs per game in 2026.In the end, it was only an infield single off the bat of Nico Hoerner that got Chicago into the hits column. Pete Crow-Armstrong, Alex Bregman, Seiya Suzuki — none of them could get anything going against King's deep pitch mix.Eight strikeouts for Michael King 🔥He's through seven shutout innings! pic.twitter.com/KqUO5miIq7— MLB (@MLB) September 30, 2026 Getting 17 whiffs was impressive for King, but just as effective were 20 called strikes. Chicago is one of the most patient lineups in MLB, and King made them pay for that strength by sneaking sinker after sinker into the zone early in the count to build a quick advantage.The Padres clearly wanted to get him a no-hitter, in addition to the win. We know that because the most frustration any of their players showed all night came from Manny Machado after he failed to get a hold of that Hoerner single. The former Gold Glover was visibly furious with himself as he picked up the ball.Tatis, meanwhile, continued to do Tatis things. He finished the game 2-for-3 with 3 runs, 1 RBI, 1 walk, 1 stolen base and the homer to lead off the game.FERNANDO TATIS JR. ARE YOU SERIOUS?! pic.twitter.com/hsHlrxILZk— MLB (@MLB) September 30, 2026 The scene was a team giving its fans everything they wanted, all the way up the ninth inning, when San Diego brought back Joe Musgrove. The San Diego area native had not pitched since the 2024 postseason and received a standing ovation, dugout included, as he entered the game to finish off the victory.It all added up to a statement win from the Padres, who are now one win from drawing the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS. They have won 18 of their past 21 games, which does not sound like the sort of challenge a top seed is supposed to face off the bat.Follow along with Yahoo Sports for live updates, highlights and more as the San Diego Padres host the Chicago Cubs in Game 1 of the NL wild-card round.

articles.title: Padres' hometown hero Joe Musgrove pitches first game in two years
articles.summary: Joe Musgrove's first MLB game in two years was a dramatic postseason appearance.
articles.body:
SAN DIEGO — Nearly two years since his last Major League Baseball appearance, Padres pitcher Joe Musgrove made his long-awaited return to the mound, the San Diego native getting a hero's welcome at Petco Park in the NL wild card series.

Musgrove took the mount for the ninth inning with the Padres leading 8-0 and got into trouble, giving up two singles and a walk to load the bases, but escaped unscathed to secure the San Diego win in Game 1 of the best-of-three series .

Musgrove last pitched on since Oct. 2, 2024 – a playoff game against the Atlanta Braves – and missed the entire 2025 season after undergoing Tommy John surgery, experiencing setbacks in his rehab in 2026 that kept him sidelined. The Padres became optimistic he could return when he pitched in an instructional league game last Tuesday and then batting practice three days later.

Musgrove, now 33, threw the only no-hitter in franchise history in 2021. He was an All-Star in 2022 and has a 3.20 ERA in 97 starts with San Diego after coming over in a trade from the Pittsburgh Pirates before the 2021 season. articles.body:
San Diego Padres pitcher Michael King was on the way to etching his name into MLB record books, flirting with a no-hitter against the Chicago Cubs during Game 1 of the National League wild card series at Petco Park.

The dream ended on Nico Hoerner 's infield single with one out in the seventh inning, with third baseman Manny Machado unable to pick up the ball cleanly.

There have been three no-hitters in MLB postseason history, most recently the Houston Astros ' combined no-hitter in the 2022 World Series. Don Larsen (1956 perfect game) and Roy Halladay (2010) are the only other pitchers to have accomplished the feat.

King finished with eight strikeouts in 97 pitches in seven innings, getting the win in the Padres' 8-0 victory.

The Yankees would go on to defeat the Dodgers and capture the 1956 World Series pennant in seven games, winning the series 4-3 after going down 2-0 after two games.

It would take another 54 years for the second-ever no-hitter to happen. Philadelphia Phillies pitcher Roy Halladay did it in Game 1 of the National League Divisional Series against the Cincinnati Reds .

He led the Phillies to a 4-0 win at Citizens Bank Park. With Halladay leading the way, Philadelphia would eventually go on to sweep the NLDS against the Reds.

They say teamwork makes the dream work and that phrase rang true for the Houston Astros during Game 4 of the 2022 World Series against the Philadelphia Phillies .

A combination of Cristian Javier , Bryan Abreu , Rafael Montero and Ryan Pressly took over against the Phillies. Javier pitched six innings and Abreu, Montero and Pressly each took an inning for themselves.

articles.title: Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice, 2 stars with Boston roots, lead Yankees to statement win over the rival Red Sox
articles.summary: Schlittler tossed 6 1/3 scoreless. Rice went 4-for-5 with two homers. Together, they put the Yankees one win away from the ALDS and the Red Sox one loss from...
articles.body:
NEW YORK — Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice are from Massachusetts. More importantly for the New York Yankees , they're damn good baseball players.

Both Massholes delivered massive performances on Tuesday in Game 1 of the 2026 wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox . Schlittler tossed 6 1/3 scoreless and punched out 10. Rice went 4-for-5 with 2 homers and 6 RBI. The Yankees clobbered their forever rivals 9-0 in a laugher to put themselves one win from advancing to an ALDS date with the Tampa Bay Rays .

For most of this picturesque autumn night in the Bronx, Schlittler was the main character. It was the second consecutive postseason in which New York's flame-throwing string-bean right-hander gave his boyhood team a baseball swirly. The presumptive AL Cy Young surrendered just two hits — one to the second batter he faced and one to the last. Otherwise, Schlittler was nearly flawless, with a fifth-inning free pass to Jarren Duran the only blemish.

He did so with a barrage of curveballs, 32 to be exact, 12 more than he'd thrown in any other MLB start. That pitch-mix pivot kept Sox hitters guessing and led to a whopping 24 whiffs against Schlittler. The dominance was so striking that New York's outfielders — Cody Bellinger , Spencer Jones and Heliot Ramos — each handled the baseball just once while Schlittler was on the mound.

"It's insane, bro," Jones told Yahoo Sports postgame. "Obviously I'm locked in, ready to make plays and whatever, but six or seven pitches will happen with Cam, and I won't even think about it. I got one fly ball. Didn't touch another one."

"It's kinda boring sometimes," Ramos joked. "Like, is it time to go home yet?"

Nobody in attendance, Red Sox hitters included, was shocked to see the Yankees ace toss a gem. All season, Schlittler has bullied opponents with triple-digit heat, three unique fastballs, a dastardly curveball and the spiteful aggression of a more aggrieved man. Few batted an eye when the third pitch out of his hand clocked in at 101 mph. But when the 2022 seventh-round draft pick reemerged from the Yankees' dugout for the seventh inning, with 107 pitches already on his ledger, a gleeful, unexpected roar reverberated around the ballpark.

A few batters later, Schlittler was done, but the night was his nonetheless. He finished with 117 pitches, the most by a Yankee in a postseason start since CC Sabathia way back in the 2012 ALDS. Simply put: Pitchers don't really do that anymore. In the era of big velocity and deep bullpens, teams rarely let starters wander far past the 100-pitch mark. In fact, the only other 117-pitch playoff start since 2019 was Garrett Crochet 's wild-card Game 1 performance against the Yankees last year in this very ballyard.

That one was a crowd-silencer. This one was a lot more thunderous.

"Any time he's going out there, he's got the most confidence," catcher Austin Wells said of Schlittler. "Now, back to back years, great outings against them in the playoffs. That's just what he's going to do."

It was clear leading into Tuesday's showdown that Boston's offensive approach against Schlittler would revolve around working deep counts and grinding out at-bats. Red Sox skipper Chad Tracy said as much during his Monday media conference. Maybe they wouldn't rain runs on Schlittler's head, but they could certainly attempt to outlast him in a war of attrition. After all, only one qualified MLB starter allowed foul balls at a higher rate this year. Drag Schlittler into the mud, force him to the showers after five, and Boston could take its best shot against the underbelly of New York's bullpen.

The second Boston hitter of the night, catcher Adley Rutschman , used that strategy to perfection. He worked a 10-pitch plate appearance against Schlittler before dunking a single into left. It was the type of battle that threatened to shorten the hurler's evening. Yet Schlittler kept on pitching, kept on blowing gas by a carousel of overmatched Red Sox. By the time Boston got a clean frame against a more mortal arm, they faced too steep a climb — a four-run deficit with just six outs to go.

That strong Yankees advantage was mostly Rice's doing. He smoked a solo shot to dead center in the fifth, doubling New York's lead to two. A few innings later, Rice laced a single into right and plated the third Yankees run. Then, in the eighth, Rice delivered the final blow: a no-doubt grand slam into the home bullpen that sent Yankee Stadium into full, ear-splitting revelry.

Much has been made about Schlittler's and Rice's Massachusetts origins, how Rice grew up a Yankees fan in Sox country, how Schlittler pours fuel on his competitive fire by sparring with Sox fans online. But the real story is how two overlooked, late-drafted, small-school college players developed into franchise-altering monsters. Schlittler was a seventh-rounder out of Northeastern; Rice went in the 12th from Dartmouth. Besides, none of the players in Boston's clubhouse care that the two dudes who kicked their butts on Tuesday happen to be from Massachusetts.

It's no surprise, then, that when asked about Schlittler's and Rice's New England connection after the game, Boone directed his answer toward otherwise forgotten chunks of the 2021 and 2022 MLB drafts.

"Pretty remarkable. I mean, not two top-draft-pick guys. Obviously with strong Massachusetts ties. Obviously, that's been a storyline for a couple of years now," he said. "For them to go out and have that kind of night together to start this postseason, pretty amazing."

Schlittler conveyed a similar sentiment. "Mid-round guys ..." he said. "Just to have the confidence of being mid-round guys, having to work a little bit harder to get up here and embrace that together, it's special."

It's also a testament to the Yankees' scouting and development operation. Every single MLB organization had access to Schlittler and Rice. For all of New York's financial might, identifying and empowering homegrown players has been an enormous part of their sustained success. Most of the Yankees' evaluators and coaches who discovered, advocated for and molded Schlittler and Rice probably don't care that the duo grew up in the shadow of Fenway.

Talent is talent, no matter where it comes from. If you can ball, you can ball.

articles.title: Schlittler and Rice torment hometown team as Yankees beat rival Red Sox 9-0 in playoff opener
articles.summary: New York outhit Boston 12-3 in the fifth postseason shutout since 2002 for the Yankees, who led the majors in ERA this year for the first time since 1957.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Back in Boston, they’re the two that got away. Cam Schlittler pitched another playoff gem against the Red Sox, and Ben Rice also burned their hometown team with a late grand slam and six RBIs as the New York Yankees opened this Wild Card Series rematch by romping to a 9-0 victory Tuesday night. With the Yankees minus star slugger Aaron Judge because of a calf injury, Rice homered twice, doubled and had four hits to power the offense. Schlittler, a clear frontrunner for the AL Cy Young Award, struck out 10 in a dominant performance reminiscent of the one that ended Boston’s season last year. Rice and Schlittler were both raised among Red Sox fans in Massachusetts and went to college in New England before getting plucked by the Yankees out of Boston’s backyard in baseball’s amateur draft. “Pretty remarkable,” New York manager Aaron Boone said. “Obviously that’s been a storyline for a couple of years now. For them to go out and have that kind of night together to start this postseason, pretty amazing and kind of hard to grasp a little bit, frankly, but I’m certainly glad we have those two.” Rice was actually a Yankees fan while growing up outside Boston. “Wearing the Yankees jersey to the first-grade picture day probably got some weird looks,” he said. “Definitely adds, like, a cool little layer to it, and for Cam, too. It’s always fun playing against them. And having a solid game against them is pretty cool.” No. 9 batter Austin Wells drove in two runs and 21-year-old rookie George Lombard Jr. had three hits for New York in his postseason debut. Schlittler, who led the American League with a 1.95 ERA, allowed only two singles and one walk in 6 1/3 innings without letting a runner reach second base. He threw 117 pitches — 10 more than his previous career high and most by a Yankees postseason starter since Hall of Fame lefty CC Sabathia threw 121 in the 2012 AL Division Series against Baltimore. “I got a little greedy,” Boone said. The major league high this season was 120 by Dylan Cease for Toronto at Boston in July. The 25-year-old Schlittler retired 13 straight batters before a two-out walk in the fifth, bringing several chants of “MVP! MVP!” from the sellout crowd of 48,437 in the Bronx. He walked off the mound to a standing ovation after yielding a one-out single in the seventh, and Paul Blackburn promptly got Ceddanne Rafaela to ground into an inning-ending double play that preserved a 2-0 lead. New York outhit Boston 12-3 in the fifth postseason shutout since 2002 for the Yankees, who led the majors in ERA this year for the first time since 1957. Game 2 in the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium is Wednesday night, when a victory would send New York into a best-of-five Division Series against AL East champion Tampa Bay. Going into this postseason, Game 1 winners had advanced 15 times in the 16 best-of-three Wild Card Series since the format was implemented in 2022. The only exception was the Red Sox last year. Boston and New York have split six previous postseason matchups. The Yankees took last year’s Wild Card Series between the longtime rivals on the strength of Schlittler’s dominant performance in Game 3, when the rookie struck out 12 over eight innings in a 4-0 win. Schlittler has said he received on-line abuse before some of his outings against Boston. He’s used it as motivation. The right-hander is 4-1 with a 0.47 ERA and 49 strikeouts in six career starts against the Red Sox — including the playoffs. “It’s very well known that if you want to be a legend, which is obviously the goal, you’ve got to do it in the postseason,” Schlittler said. Rice gave the Yankees a 2-0 lead with a 423-foot solo homer into Monument Park in straightaway center field on the third pitch from left-handed reliever Erik Miller, who replaced Payton Tolle with two outs in the fifth after the rookie starter threw 83 pitches. The 27-year-old Rice added a run-scoring single with the bases loaded in the seventh and a grand slam to right-center that capped a five-run eighth. The 16th slam in Yankees postseason history gave Rice six RBIs, matching the franchise record for a postseason game accomplished by four other players. Rice also homered in Game 2 of last year’s Wild Card Series. He led New York with 41 homers, 97 RBIs and an .897 OPS this year in his third major league season. “I’ll remember getting a W versus the Red Sox. There’s nothing better than that,” Rice said. “I’ll remember Cam going out there and just being lights out, like he always is. I’ll remember the atmosphere. It was just an awesome night. Great way to kick off the series.”

articles.title: In 2025, Jake Burger and wife Ashlyn launched a foundation after daughter Penelope was born with Down syndrome; within months, it raised over $150,000
articles.summary: Jake and Ashlyn Burger established the Burger Family Foundation to support families impacted by Down syndrome. Following the birth of their daughter Penelope, the foundation has raised over $150,000 for awareness and direct assistance programs such as Pens Pearls. Their efforts also include community initiatives and employment opportunities for adults with disabilities.
articles.body: Jake Burger and Ashlyn Burger have taken their experience as parents and turned it into a growing philanthropic effort on behalf of Down syndrome awareness, financial assistance and inclusion. The Burger Family Foundation was established in March 2025, a few months after their daughter Penelope was born with Down syndrome in October 2024. The foundation was established to assist families who experience the costs and challenges that can accompany raising a child with a disability.The Major League Baseball Foundation says it raised more than $150,000 in its first year alone with its “Down Syndrome Is Cool” merchandise campaign. The campaign combines fundraising and awareness, leveraging apparel and accessories to initiate discussions on Down syndrome and inclusion. The organization has also expanded its work beyond fundraising through direct family support, community events and its Lucky Ranch initiative.Jake Burger and Ashlyn Burger build foundationJake and Ashlyn Burger launched the Burger Family Foundation on March 21, 2025, World Down Syndrome Day. The organization was started because of Penelope’s inspiration to help other families going through similar struggles. Its stated mission is to provide direct financial assistance, therapy, involvement in the community and ranch-life-related activities.The foundation’s financial assistance program, Pens Pearls, is named after Penelope and provides direct support to families with disability-related needs. The program has already distributed more than $40,000 directly to families seeking help for specialized therapy services, MLB said. The foundation also says Pens Pearls is a way to help meet basic needs, services and opportunities for children with disabilities.Since then, the organization has broadened its work to include employment and community initiatives. NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WMOT) Nashville, Tenn. A multi-acre facility is being developed in Nashville, Tenn., with the hope of providing jobs for adults with disabilities. The first phase is poultry operations, and partnerships with Nashville businesses are being used to help support wages for employees with disabilities.Texas Rangers infielder Jake Burger balances baseball and advocacyJake Burger’s tenure with the foundation has overlapped with his time with the Texas Rangers. When Burger arrived in Texas prior to the 2025 season, he changed his jersey number to 21 in honor of Penelope. The number refers to Trisomy 21, the clinical term for Down syndrome.Burger was a standout member of the Texas Rangers lineup during the 2026 regular season on the field. MLB has him playing 155 games with 28 homers, 90 RBIs and a .228 batting average. His 28 home runs ranked among the American League leaders, and his 90 RBIs put him among the leading run producers in the league.Burger has also used his MLB platform to raise awareness for Down syndrome organizations. On road trips, he has traveled the country visiting GiGi’s Playhouse Down Syndrome Achievement Centers, and he and Ashlyn have participated in fundraising efforts to expand services in the Dallas-Fort Worth area.The Texas Rangers have backed some of these efforts. Globe Life Field has held Down Syndrome Awareness Day in back-to-back seasons, with proceeds from specialty tickets and merchandise benefiting local Down syndrome organizations and the foundation’s Pens Pearls program. The foundation has also received some of the proceeds from the sale of Jake Burger jerseys at Globe Life Field.Jake Burger and Ashlyn Burger bring community togetherThe foundation has also organized large-scale fundraising events that combine entertainment with awareness. Nashville hosted the first Lucky Classic celebrity softball game and home run derby in November 2025 featuring MLB players, musicians and other celebrities, as well as honorary participants with Down syndrome. Over 2,500 tickets were sold for the first event.The event became a major fundraising event for the foundation. The first Lucky Classic raised more than $250,000 for its work supporting families and creating opportunities for people with Down syndrome, MLB said. The event involved players and celebrities from the entertainment and sports worlds, adding yet another way for the foundation to combine fundraising with public awareness.The Burgers have continued to build the foundation for direct aid and broader involvement in the community. The “Down Syndrome Is Cool” merchandise campaign has raised more than $150,000, and Down Syndrome Awareness Day events have brought fans into the fundraiser at Globe Life Field. The foundation has also been helped by the Texas Rangers organization and the Players Trust.In May 2026, The Players Trust named Jake Burger its Most Valuable Philanthropist honoree and awarded the Foundation a $10,000 grant from the Players Trust for the Lucky Ranch project. The recognition came after the couple continued their work with families, disability organizations and community programs.The foundation’s progress also highlights a broader shift from raising awareness to offering concrete support. Pens Pearls is providing direct financial support, and Lucky Ranch is equipped to offer job opportunities for adults with disabilities. Those initiatives together represent the two core areas of the Burgers’ work: addressing the immediate needs of families and building longer-term opportunities for people with disabilities.For Jake Burger and Ashlyn Burger, the foundation was built on the arrival of Penelope and the experience of navigating Down syndrome as a family. Since its inception in 2025, the organization has grown into a fundraising and community effort that offers financial aid, awareness initiatives, employment opportunities and major events. articles.title: Making the Case For 5 Teams That Can Dethrone the Playoff Dodgers and Save MLB
articles.summary: The last time Major League Baseball fans desperately needed saving from an evil empire, Luis Gonzalez and the 2001 Arizona Diamondbacks delivered one of the most unforgettable knockout punches in postseason history.
articles.body:
The last time Major League Baseball fans desperately needed saving from an evil empire, Luis Gonzalez and the 2001 Arizona Diamondbacks delivered one of the most unforgettable knockout punches in postseason history.

Who, pray tell, has the best chance of saving us from a Los Angeles Dodgers three-peat that could drive even more of a wedge into the forthcoming labor negotiations?

From a purely financial perspective, the Cleveland Guardians and their $93M payroll trouncing the Dodgers in the World Series would be perfektenschlag . The $114M Tampa Bay Rays or $117M Chicago White Sox doing so would also be objectively incredible.

However, our ranking of the five teams best equipped to dethrone the Dodgers has nothing to do with payroll and everything to do with matchups.

What Are the Dodgers' Potentially Fatal Flaws?

Los Angeles won 100 regular season games, including 18 of its final 23.

That's more than the Dodgers won in either of the previous two regular seasons, and also their most scorching-hot September surge yet in this dynastic run.

However, they lost 62 times, finished with merely the second-best record this season and actually kind of stunk for about eight weeks before reigniting over Labor Day weekend.

For starters, neither Shohei Ohtani nor Freddie Freeman has looked right in a while.

The former's injuries and struggles have been documented ad nauseam, culminating in a .503 OPS over his final 18 games, last homering on August 18. The latter more quietly vanished, playing in nearly every game, but homering just once in his 277 plate appearances since July 4.

That left-handed duo has combined for 60 hits, 17 home runs and 40 RBI over the past two postseasons. Even though Mookie Betts and Kyle Tucker woke up in a massive way in September, the Dodgers are nowhere near as intimidating if Ohtani and Freeman continue to struggle.

Second, Blake Snell's health is questionable yet again.

Snell left his Sept. 16 start after one inning with a groin strain.

He did pitch four innings against the Giants 10 days later. He was pumping in his four-seamer faster in that start than he had been all season. But it has been one setback after another for Snell, who was such a huge part of their postseason run one year ago. He had been on fire in his six starts prior to the most recent injury.

It's preposterous that a team that already doesn't have Ohtani pitching and doesn't know what to expect from Snell still gets to roll with Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow in its first three games. If Snell isn't his usual self, that's an opening for an opponent.

For the year, the Dodgers have a +201 run differential, which rates second-best in the majors.

Between the seventh and eighth innings, they're sitting at a +1.

Edwin Díaz appears to have turned a corner with five scoreless innings to close out the regular season, but can they possibly have any faith in him in October when he had a 17.65 ERA across his previous 11 appearances?

Tanner Scott has done fine in the closer role this season, but he has two blown saves and two other losses across his last 13 appearances. Outside of the two Chicago teams, he's arguably the least trustworthy closer in this postseason.

The Dodgers do have a whole bunch of "good enough" relievers. In fact, all nine Dodgers pitchers with at least 27 relief appearances this season have an ERA between 2.64 and 3.89. But once the starter reaches the end of his rope, there's not a single arm coming out of this bullpen that feels impenetrable.

Say this much for Atlanta: It had the Dodgers' number during the regular season, going 5-1 in the head-to-head series.

However, Milwaukee was 6-0 against the Dodgers during the 2025 regular season before LA swept the Brewers in the NLCS, so it's going to take more than that to make the argument here.

What's a bummer for #BravesCountry is that Chris Sale—who tossed a complete-game shutout against the Dodgers a month ago—is pitching on Tuesday against Philadelphia, which means he won't be available until Game 2 of the NLDS against Los Angeles. Even that will be on just four days' rest, which he hasn't done since early April. If there is a Game 5, it would presumably be up to Sale on four days' rest yet again.

Is Tyler Mahle—who has never pitched in the postseason, but who became Atlanta's clear No. 2 starter after the trade deadline—ready for the spotlight?

Most importantly, can the Braves' bats wake back up?

Potent offense spearheaded their early run to a 36-16 record, but Atlanta averaged just 3.7 runs while playing basically .500 baseball over the final eight weeks of the regular season.

We all know how streaky Matt Olson can be, though. It sure would be something if the guy Atlanta traded for to replace Freddie Freeman—who was so huge for the Braves in the 2021 NLCS against the Dodgers—caught fire and sent Freeman and Co. home early.

It would also be something if Atlanta pummeled Tarik Skubal whenever he starts in the NLDS. There was a lot of speculation leading up to the trade deadline that if he didn't end up with the Dodgers, he might go to the Braves. Maybe they can use that as motivation to rally the troops against him?

Should we get a rematch of the 2020 World Series, could the Rays flip the script and win their first-ever title?

While going up against Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, who combined to make four starts for them in that Fall Classic six years ago?

Those particular matchups would be wildly intriguing.

Glasnow has faced every other team in the majors at least twice in his career, but he has never once pitched against Tampa Bay. Meanwhile, Snell has faced the Rays three times in his career and has a worse ERA (6.00) against them than he does against any other team.

To be fair, if we're going to play that game, we should also note that Tarik Skubal has eviscerated the Rays with a 0.74 ERA over his five starts against them.

There's just something about that "They pitched for us last time!" dynamic—even though Junior Caminero was perhaps still learning how to drive at the time—that could spark a real fire.

Beyond that, the Rays have made the transition from "fun story" to "serious World Series threat" over the past two months.

Even with both Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda—who co-carried the offense with Caminero through the first half—coming back to earth in a big way, Tampa Bay has had maybe the most well-rounded offenses since the All-Star Break.

Victor Mesa Jr. is threatening to be the rookie-in-the-postseason star that Randy Arozarena was in 2020. How can you not be romantic about a team that has three of the four players (Chandler Simpson, Cedric Mullins and Taylor Walls) with at least 10 bunt singles this season? They might mess around and lay down three bunts in a single inning and just glitch the Dodgers' brains.

Heading into the postseason, San Diego was the only team hotter than the Dodgers. The Padres won 17 of their final 20 games, including taking two out of three from the Dodgers in Los Angeles.

If you think they're hot now, imagine how we'll feel about this team in two weeks if they can set up an NLCS showdown with their NL West rivals by plowing through the Cubs and Brewers in the first two rounds.

They won't be scared of the Dodgers, either. They want all of that smoke, as evidenced by their NLDS clashes in both 2022 and 2024—San Diego taking the former in four games and Los Angeles surviving the latter in five.

The extremely debatable part is whether the Padres' starting rotation can keep things interesting and hand enough leads to one of the best bullpens in baseball.

Even in that late September series in LA, ace Michael King allowed five earned runs in four innings of work, Nick Pivetta failed to complete five innings and Robbie Ray didn't even make it out of the fourth. That's probably not going to be enough in a best-of-seven showdown.

But if Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill stay red hot, there's a decent chance that San Diego scores its sweetest postseason series win in franchise history.

Quite the "out of the frying pan and into the fire" proposal here. Having the Yankees save us from the Dodgers dynasty would be like bringing in snakes to deal with a scorpion problem. But one problem at a time, right?

For most MLB hitters, facing Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell in consecutive games is a slump waiting to happen.

For Paul Goldschmidt, however, that sounds like an all-you-can-eat buffet.

In 32 career plate appearances against that trio, Goldy has gone 12-for-27 with five home runs, one double and five walks.

The Yankees most likely bench him for the game against Yoshinobu Yamamoto, but Goldschmidt could really set the tone early as the leadoff hitter against the other three aces.

Speaking of aces, the Yankees are the one team that could go toe-to-toe with the Dodgers' rotation.

Cam Schlitter vs. Yamamoto. Max Fried vs. Skubal. Gerrit Cole vs. Glasnow. Carlos Rodón vs. Snell.

Every one of those matchups could be legendary. That's a substantial difference from the 2024 World Series, in which Clarke Schmidt, Luis Gil, Walker Buehler and Ben Casparius each got a start in a five-game series that featured 16 home runs.

New York's biggest edge, though, could be in the bullpen, if Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn and David Bednar have one more dynamite month left in the tank.

Moreover, the Yankees have done their best offensive work in the seventh and eighth innings this season, which we previously mentioned is where the Dodgers have been most vulnerable.

Milwaukee lost a seven-game battle to the Dodgers in the 2018 NLCS and was later swept by LA in both the 2020 wild card round and the 2025 NLCS. Those have been their only meetings in postseason history.

However, the Brewers have never been this good.

Yes, they were the NL's No. 1 seed for both the 2018 and 2025 showdowns, but their pitching is so much better this year than it was in 2018. After limping to the finish line with a 19-21 record down the stretch last year, they went an MLB-best 29-12 in their final 41 games this time around—a stretch that began with a season-defining series in Los Angeles, taking three out of four from the Dodgers.

Milwaukee's season-long lack of home runs is definitely a concern. Only Toronto (152) ended the regular season with fewer dingers than Milwaukee's 154. Though they held the Dodgers to 3.75 runs per game in the 2025 NLCS, their inability to put runs on the board doomed them.

Maybe their small ball approach works better this time around? They did rank second in the majors in scoring, after all, while leading the majors in on-base percentage.

The bigger question, though, is whether the non-Jacob Misiorowski portion of the starting rotation can hold a candle to what the Dodgers will bring to the table.

Logan Henderson has had a fantastic season, including two strong starts against the Dodgers. He will presumably be No. 2 in their postseason rotation.

However, Kyle Harrison went from "maybe should have been an All-Star" in the first half to a train wreck with an 8.67 ERA over his last 10 appearances. At this point, it's probably Robert Gasser in Game 3 and a Dustin May/Shane Drohan piggyback in Game 4, neither of which is a promising counter to Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell.

But if anyone is going to go full "2014 Madison Bumgarner" and just carry his team to a World Series with gem after gem, it's probably going to be Misiorowski.

articles.title: Astros Pitcher 'Pretty Pissed Off' by Fans' Boos During Game 1 Loss to White Sox in MLB Playoffs
articles.summary: In the aftermath of their 6-3 loss to the Chicago White Sox in Game 1 of the American League Wild Card series on Tuesday, members of the Houston Astros aired some of their frustration at the home fans for greeting them with boos at one point.
articles.body:
In the aftermath of their 6-3 loss to the Chicago White Sox in Game 1 of the American League Wild Card series on Tuesday, members of the Houston Astros aired some of their frustration at the home fans for greeting them with boos at one point.

Astros reliever Bennett Sousa told reporters after the game he is "pretty pissed off" when the fans began booing them in the seventh inning.

Sousa was also just generally unhappy with the apparent apathy from the hometown crowd throughout the game:

"The fans here are definitely spoiled with a lot of ALCS and World Series runs, and we have to earn that right to bring this team back to that position. That being said, when this team was in their first (playoff) series 10 years ago, Minute Maid Park was probably packed. It makes a big difference. If we were in Chicago, it'd probably be loud as s--t."

One part of Sousa's complaint was around the fact Daikin Park wasn't sold out for this game. The announced crowd was 34,011, nearly 7,000 below the capacity of 40,963.

Sam Gonzalez Kelly of the Houston Chronicle noted how little fan interest there seemed to be around the city.

There are any number of reasons for the low attendance figure for a playoff game. First pitch was at 4:10 p.m. local time on a Tuesday afternoon for a matchup that was only set on Sunday evening.

Perhaps the biggest issue, though, is this Astros team has a case as the worst playoff team in MLB history. Their 81 wins in the regular season are the fewest in a 162-game season for a team that made the postseason.

Houston's minus-32 run differential is the third-worst by a playoff team in a 162-game season, ahead of only the 2005 San Diego Padres (minus-42) and 2023 Miami Marlins (minus-57).

Last season was the unofficial end of the Astros' near-dynastic run when they missed the playoffs for the first time since 2016. During the eight seasons from 2017 to '24, they played in the ALCS seven times, world Series four times and won two championships.

Sousa and other Astros players are certainly right to be unhappy that fans don't seem eager to support this group in a playoff game, but they also have to give them a reason to be excited about watching them play.

We will see if the mood in Daikin Park changes on Wednesday when the Astros look to keep their season alive in Game 2 against the White Sox.

articles.title: Fernando Tatis Jr. Talks Padres' Dominant MLB Playoffs G1 Win vs. Cubs, 'Beautiful Baseball Night'
articles.summary: Fernando Tatís Jr. reflected on what was essentially a perfect night for the San Diego Padres on Tuesday, as they cruised to an 8-0 win over the Chicago Cubs in Game 1 of their National League Wild Card Series.
articles.body:
Fernando Tatís Jr. reflected on what was essentially a perfect night for the San Diego Padres on Tuesday, as they cruised to an 8-0 win over the Chicago Cubs in Game 1 of their National League Wild Card Series.

Speaking to reporters following the one-sided victory, Tatís said, "We couldn't have scripted it any better than what happened tonight. Today was a beautiful baseball night for every San Diegan."

Playing in front of over 47,000 fans at Petco Park in San Diego, the Padres poured it on from the get-go, as they led 2-0 after one inning and 7-0 through five.

Tatís was a big part of the Padres' offensive success in Game 1, as he launched a solo home run to lead off the bottom of the first inning.

All told, Tatís went 2-for-3, walked once, stole a base and scored three runs to go along with the one homer and one RBI.

Veteran third baseman Manny Machado also homered and drove in a pair, while starting pitcher Michael King authored a masterpiece, allowing one hit and no runs, while walking three and striking out eight over seven innings.

King and the San Diego pitching staff notably shut down Cubs outfielder and NL MVP front-runner Pete Crow-Armstrong, as he went 0-for-3 with three strikeouts and one walk.

The Padres are now just one win away from advancing to the National League Division Series for the second time in the past three seasons.

They will send Nick Pivetta to the mound for Wednesday night's Game 2 of the NLWCS, while Chicago will counter with Kevin Gausman.

articles.title: Milwaukee Brewers: 3 players that must stay hot for October MLB Postseason run
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers finished the 2026 MLB regular season with the best record in baseball for the second year in a row. Their 103-59 mark gave them a fourt...
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers finished the 2026 MLB regular season with the best record in baseball for the second year in a row. Their 103-59 mark gave them a fourth consecutive National League Central Division title, a division they won by 14 games this year, and has them sitting as the number one seed in the postseason.

As such, the Brewers have this week off before the start of the National League Division Series on Saturday. They will play the winner of the Wild Card Series between the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres . Last night, San Diego won the first game 8-0 and could eliminate Chicago from the postseason as early as tonight.

3 Milwaukee Brewers players that must stay hot no matter what opponent they face

There are many Brewers fans who, while delighted to see the hated Cubs lose so emphatically, are not exactly thrilled about the prospect of facing the red-hot Padres. Indeed, San Diego has been the best team in baseball for about a month, and there is a fear that they could knock Milwaukee out early.

In order to be the best, though, a team has to beat the best. The Brewers have everything they need to beat anyone, including San Diego. That being said, these three players continuing their brilliant play from September would go a long way to ensuring that happens.

Playing just his third MLB season, Jackson Chourio is already tied for the franchise record in career postseason home runs. Clearly, Milwaukee would love to see that trend continue in the NLDS and beyond.

Chourio has certainly set himself up for a strong showing the playoffs. He ended the 2026 season by hitting .337/.389/.531 with five home runs, 18 RBI, and nine stolen bases in September. That is certainly the kind of production in October, too.

Overall, Chourio hit .291/.351/.487 with 25 home runs, 75 RBI, 23 stolen bases, and 96 runs scored. What is so amazing about these numbers is that he missed the first month of the year with a hairline fracture in his left hand.

If he can continue his hot streak in the postseason, it will be hard to count the Brewers out of any playoff series.

Following the All-Star Break, catcher William Contreras went through a prolonged slump at the plate that saw him dropped in the batting order. While Milwaukee kept winning games, their offense was not as productive. This past month, though, saw Contreras hit .263/.330/.513 with five home runs and 24 RBI.

While his batting average and on-base percentage were lower than his overall season marks (.270/.341/.417), his OPS was almost 100 points higher. This is because his 10 extra base hits in September tied for the most he had in any month this season (he also had 10 in April).

The Brewers will certainly need him driving him runs in the middle of the order if they are to make a deep run again this year.

After a career year in 2025, Brice Turang was even better in 2026 hitting .268/.366/.450 with career highs in home runs (21), RBI (100), and runs (102).

These final numbers are all the more impressive considering that he hit .175/.266/.247 in August.

A strong September, though, put Turang back on track and he is carrying some great momentum going into the postseason. This past month, he hit .361/.475/.602 with four home runs and 22 RBI.

The Brewers will hope that kind of production continues at the top of their lineup this October.

articles.title: Why You Should Believe Tom Pohlad When He Says Twins Plan to Spend Big
articles.summary: The Minnesota Twins offseason is upon us and, yet again, Tom Pohlad is making big promises... that he will probably have to keep.
articles.body:
The MLB playoffs began today. For those who stopped paying attention weeks or even months ago, the Minnesota Twins ' 2026 season has been over for a couple of days. The Twins completed their schedule on Sunday, with a home victory over the Texas Rangers , cementing their regular season record at 77-85.

Thus, the Twins will watch the 2026 playoffs from the couch, just like us. Then, we enter one of the most important offseasons in Major League Baseball history.

The current MLB collective bargaining agreement (CBA) expires Dec. 1, and there is very little hope right now that we'll be able to avoid the league's fifth-ever owner-initiated lockout.

More on that shortly, because it's an important part of this story.

For now, let's stay in the moment and turn focus back to Target Field, where today, Minnesota Twins controlling owner Tom Pohlad met with reporters and ( yet again ) took the conversation to places we never saw from the Pohlads before his arrival.

Tom Pohlad making big Minnesota Twins payroll promises again

Obviously, all eyes are on Pohlad's pocketbook this offseason. He's been telling us since he took over as team president that he intends to spend whatever necessary — but only when the timing is right.

Naturally, now that the 2026 season has come to an end, reporters followed up on that notion Tuesday. Is the time to spend now?

Lo and behold, though he refused to give any specific numbers, Tom doubled down on his past promises and told gathered media that "a $100 million payroll or anything close to that is not sufficient to be consistently competitive and in the playoffs."

"I have said over and over that a $100 million payroll or anything close to that is not sufficient to be consistently competitive and in the playoffs, and so we intend to take the offseason and meaningfully invest. I know that everybody in this room wants to understand, wants me to define what "meaningfully" is, and I understand that that's a subjective word. But I am confident that [Jeremy Zoll], if he has conviction about a move that's going to improve this roster and help us accomplish our goals, that this ownership group is prepared to support him with the financial resources he needs." Tom Pohlad on the MN Twins' spending plans this offseason

"I have said over and over that a $100 million payroll or anything close to that is not sufficient to be consistently competitive and in the playoffs, and so we intend to take the offseason and meaningfully invest. I know that everybody in this room wants to understand, wants me to define what "meaningfully" is, and I understand that that's a subjective word. But I am confident that [Jeremy Zoll], if he has conviction about a move that's going to improve this roster and help us accomplish our goals, that this ownership group is prepared to support him with the financial resources he needs."

Tom Pohlad on the MN Twins' spending plans this offseason

Pohlad offered few details into what exactly he has in store for this offseason. What he made clear, however, is that the Minnesota Twins plan to spend this offseason, and they aren't afraid to show it.

How aggressive that is likely depends on what type of opportunities present themselves. At this point, I believe the Twins plan to have a higher payroll next season than ever before.

What Tom Pohlad won't tell you though… is that he probably won't have a choice. And that brings us back to the MLB's CBA negotiations.

Twins will probably spend more money this offseason, but not by choice

Essentially, MLB owners want a salary cap and the players are determined to fight against it, even if it means missing paychecks. Thus, a lockout on December 1 feels inevitable.

The better question, at this point, is how long said lockout will last. Over the weekend, the President of the United States was even asked if he'd be willing to step in and help Major League Baseball, if necessary.

President Trump says he would consider stepping in to prevent a MLB lockout if given the opportunity: "I would do it if it was appropriate. I would certainly do it if I could… If I could help, I'd love to help." pic.twitter.com/U7zdAeGxAG — Punchoutpitch (@Punchoutpitch) September 27, 2026

President Trump says he would consider stepping in to prevent a MLB lockout if given the opportunity: "I would do it if it was appropriate. I would certainly do it if I could… If I could help, I'd love to help." pic.twitter.com/U7zdAeGxAG

Punchoutpitch (@Punchoutpitch) September 27, 2026

It's way too early to tell which side will come out on top, or how long it will take for a new Collective Bargaining Agreement to get finalized. But when it happens, baseball is expected to look different.

While players may object to a salary cap, they welcome some sort of salary floor, or at least some sort of worthwhile competitive balance tax that will make sure teams spend above a certain amount on player payroll every season.

For MN Twins fans desperately waiting to see the Pohlads spend money, that's music to your ears. But it gets better. Early CBA proposals that have gone back and forth between the MLB and MLB Players Association have included salary floors or competitive tax thresholds between $150 million and $171 million.

MLB is proposing a salary floor of $171.2 million and a salary cap of $245.3 million, with players receiving 50% of the revenues. Under this proposal, eight teams would have to reduce their payrolls: Dodgers , Mets , Yankees , Blue Jays, Phillies , Red Sox , Padres and Braves. Would… pic.twitter.com/CryQDN5kAj — The Athletic (@TheAthletic) September 15, 2026

MLB is proposing a salary floor of $171.2 million and a salary cap of $245.3 million, with players receiving 50% of the revenues. Under this proposal, eight teams would have to reduce their payrolls: Dodgers , Mets , Yankees , Blue Jays, Phillies , Red Sox , Padres and Braves. Would… pic.twitter.com/CryQDN5kAj

The Athletic (@TheAthletic) September 15, 2026

How much money could the MN Twins be forced to spend?

For context, the most expensive Minnesota Twins roster ever played in 2023, right before the Pohlads started cutting payroll. That season, the Twins paid $156 million in player salaries. Uncoincidentally, that was the same summer they advanced to the second round of the playoffs for the first time in two decades.

If MLB's future salary floor or competitive balance tax ends up even at the lowest proposed amount so far ($150 million), the Minnesota Twins (whose projected 2027 payroll currently sits at $101 million per Spotrac ) would have to add $50 million in payroll this offseason, just to climb above that number.

In other words, whenever baseball does return — if it comes back with some sort of salary floor — we can expect the Minnesota Twins to be more spend-happy than any time in franchise history. Just not out of the goodness of Tom Pohlad's heart.

#MNTwins owner Tom Pohlad reflecting on the season: "I want to thank the fans that got behind the team this year. I understand the patience in this market has run out, and I assure you we have a sense of urgency." pic.twitter.com/O0sVmyLof4 — Will Hall (@WillHallKARE11) September 29, 2026

#MNTwins owner Tom Pohlad reflecting on the season: "I want to thank the fans that got behind the team this year. I understand the patience in this market has run out, and I assure you we have a sense of urgency." pic.twitter.com/O0sVmyLof4

Will Hall (@WillHallKARE11) September 29, 2026

Does it matter whether Pohlad spends by choice or by force? Not really, as long as the Twins get to keep Joe Ryan and Ryan Jeffers deep into the future, and add more talent to boost a roster that has a core good enough that the right signings could mean an AL Central title as soon as next season.

With that being said, until a new CBA is signed that includes some sort of salary floor penalty, these are all just dreams. It's still possible we end up with little change this MLB offseason, if owners fold early during negotiations, unexpectedly.

If that were to happen, and baseball returns without a salary floor or a tax system that brutally penalizes teams who refuse to spend above it — and then the Pohlads still go out and splurge on a roster that costs $150+ million — well then I will actually be impressed by Tom Pohlad's "willingness" to spend.

However, if I had to guess, Tom probably believes that the new CBA will force him to spend… which would explain why he has been so comfortable making bold financial statements and unheard of promises about future spending. It would also tell us why he's shy about revealing any actual numbers… since those are yet to be negotiated.
